title: Comparative evaluation of sediment collection and extraction protocols for environmental DNA metabarcoding of benthic communities in estuarine systems
content:
Sediment eDNA biodiversity patterns were driven primarily by sampling location and collection method, while extraction approach had little effect after successful amplification. Combining replicate 250 mg scoops with 10 g sieved sediment may improve monitoring reliability for Estuarine systems like the Indian River Lagoon.


Abstract

Coastal and estuarine monitoring programmes increasingly use environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding for benthic monitoring, yet standardized protocols for sediment collection, extraction and processing remain limited. Moreover, any proposed standardized method needs to be tested in a particular study system to validate across various grain sizes, salinities, climate regimes and species richness gradients. This study evaluated how sediment collection method (Ponar grab sieved, Ponar grab scoop and internal core), processing method (homogenized vs. whole) and DNA extraction kits (250 mg Qiagen DNeasy PowerSoil Pro and 10 g Qiagen DNeasy PowerMax Soil) influence amplification success, alpha diversity and community composition using COI metabarcoding across four ecologically distinct sites in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) and adjacent St. Lucie Estuary (SLE). Amplification success varied by site and sampling method, with Ponar sieved samples from low-biomass sites only having successful amplification with the 10 g kit, demonstrating that small-volume extractions are vulnerable to low template input. Alpha diversity differed among sites and was influenced primarily by sampling method rather than extraction protocol. Sediment environmental DNA community composition showed clear separation among sites, supporting that estuarine environmental gradients drive species distributions. In contrast, extraction kit, sample mass, homogenization and DNA pooling had no significant effect on alpha diversity once amplification was successful. Sampling method also influenced local community signal: replicate sieved samples were representative, yet more variable, whereas cores and scoops were highly similar within sites. These results highlight that sampling location, and sampling methods are the dominant drivers of biodiversity patterns recovered using sediment eDNA metabarcoding in subtropical estuarine systems. Practical implications. Standardized sediment eDNA monitoring should prioritize sampling design to ensure reliable biodiversity detection. For initial implementation in benthic eDNA monitoring programmes, we recommend combining multiple 250 mg Ponar scoop samples with concurrent homogenized 10 g sieved Ponar grab samples to capture a more comprehensive profile of benthic biodiversity while maximizing cost-effectiveness and reliability. Following preliminary assessment, sampling effort can be fine-tuned to local conditions.
